# Dashboard Executive Summary — Auto-Generated

**Project:** NovaTech Revenue Intelligence Dashboard
**Analyst:** Muhammad Irfan bin Zulkifle
**Date:** 12 September 2026

The text in Part 1 is reproduced verbatim as generated by the Amazon Quick Executive Summary
feature on the published dashboard. Part 2 is my verification of it against the source data.

---

# Part 1 — Generated text (verbatim)

## Marketing Funnel
The sheet provides a comprehensive overview of lead generation, campaign performance, and channel efficiency across 2,240 total leads with $12,359,497 in campaign spend.

Direct Mail achieves the highest conversion rate at 49.0%, nearly doubling Partner Referral at 31.1%, despite Organic Search being the most expensive channel at $256,709 per closed-won lead.

The overall Lead-to-Won Conversion rate stands at 18.4%, with 412 leads reaching Closed Won out of 2,240 total, while the majority (848) remain in the Qualified Lead stage.

NovaPulse Launch delivers the strongest ROI with $394,156.59 in attributed revenue, while NovaEdge Awareness shows poor efficiency with the lowest revenue of $34,279.64.

The overall Response Rate averages 27.2%, indicating significant room for improvement in lead engagement.

## Sales Pipeline
The sheet provides a comprehensive sales performance dashboard tracking revenue, deal metrics, win rates, and loss reasons across products and managers.

Total revenue reached $707,201 with an average won deal value of $2,245 and a 63.1% overall win rate, while NovaPulse Professional led product revenue at $208,724.

Sales cycle length surged to 90.1 days in Q1' 2025, a 65.78% increase from Q4' 2024's 54.4 days, signaling growing delays in closing deals.

Manager performance varies significantly, with David Kim leading at 70.8% win rate while Brian Nakamura trails at 50.0%.

Of 184 lost deals, No Decision Made and Poor Product Fit each accounted for 43 deals, highlighting key areas for improvement.

## Customer Health
The sheet provides a comprehensive overview of customer support operations across 85 companies, tracking 3,000 total tickets, resolution performance, sentiment analysis, and account-level risk indicators.

ACCT-041 dominates support ticket volume with 334 tickets, nearly double the next highest account (ACCT-035 at 180), signaling potential account risk.

Resolution times are remarkably uniform across priority levels—low (58.9 hrs), high (57.6 hrs), and medium (57.5 hrs)—suggesting priority classification has minimal impact on resolution speed.

Sentiment across tickets skews heavily neutral (1,953), but negative tickets (684) outnumber positive ones (304) by more than 2:1, with an overall negative sentiment rate of 22.8%.

Notifications (601) and Analytics Dashboard (597) generate the highest ticket volumes by product area, while 59 tickets remain unresolved.

# Part 2 — Analyst verification

Every figure was checked against the three source CSVs. Most are exact, including the 65.78%
increase in Part 1's Sales Pipeline section, which is correct to two decimal places. Three claims do
not hold, and one deserves particular note.

## Finding 1 — A trend asserted from a partial quarter *(Sales Pipeline)*

> *"Sales cycle length surged to 90.1 days in Q1' 2025, a 65.78% increase from Q4' 2024's 54.4 days,
> signaling growing delays in closing deals."*

The arithmetic is exact. The conclusion is not supported.

| Quarter | Deals closed | Avg days to close |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 Q4 | 96 | 54.4 |
| 2025 Q1 | **28** | 90.1 |

**Q1 2025 contains one month of data.** The dataset ends 31 January 2025, so that quarter holds 28
closed deals against 96 in the previous one. A figure drawn from a third of a quarter, on under a
third of the deal volume, cannot support "signaling growing delays."

**The same tool contradicts itself on this.** Asked directly — *"Is our sales cycle getting longer or
shorter?"* — Quick Chat grouped deals by creation cohort, found the cycle **shortening** from roughly
170 days to 40, and volunteered a caveat about survivorship bias in exactly these recent months. The
auto-generated summary, reading the same dashboard, asserts the opposite conclusion with no caveat at
all.

**This is the most useful thing in the generated summary.** Two entry points into the same product,
on the same data, produce contradictory conclusions about the same metric — and the one that appears
without being asked for is the one that is wrong. A reader who only skims the executive summary never
sees the correction.

## Finding 2 — Two different populations merged into one sentence *(Customer Health)*

> *"…a comprehensive overview of customer support operations across 85 companies, tracking 3,000
> total tickets…"*

These two numbers do not belong together. The 3,000 tickets span **100 distinct accounts**; only 85
appear in the CRM. **204 tickets belong to 15 accounts that are not among the 85.**

The summary appears to have taken the account count from the scatter plot (built on the unified
dataset, which is CRM-anchored and therefore holds 85 accounts) and the ticket count from the support
dataset (100 accounts), then combined them. Each figure is correct in isolation; the sentence is not.

## Finding 3 — Overstated comparison *(Marketing Funnel)*

> *"Direct Mail achieves the highest conversion rate at 49.0%, nearly doubling Partner Referral at
> 31.1%…"*

49.0 ÷ 31.1 = **1.58×**, not "nearly double". The ranking is right; the characterisation inflates it.

The same sentence also contains a non-sequitur — *"…despite Organic Search being the most expensive
channel at $256,709 per closed-won lead."* Both facts are true, but Direct Mail's conversion rate is
not in tension with Organic Search's cost, so "despite" connects them wrongly.

## Finding 4 — Correct interpretation, incomplete evidence *(Customer Health)*

> *"Resolution times are remarkably uniform across priority levels—low (58.9 hrs), high (57.6 hrs),
> and medium (57.5 hrs)—suggesting priority classification has minimal impact on resolution speed."*

**This reading is correct**, and it is worth flagging because it is the opposite of what Quick Chat
concluded when asked the same question in conversation. Chat said the small gap *"suggests critical
tickets may be getting prioritized appropriately."* The generated summary says priority has minimal
impact. **The summary is right and the chat was wrong**, on identical data.

One flaw remains: it lists low, high and medium but **omits critical at 56.1 hours** — the level the
finding most depends on. Critical is the fastest of the four, by 2.8 hours over low, which is what
makes the severity scale look non-functional. Leaving it out weakens a correct conclusion.

## Summary of verification

| # | Claim | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sales cycle "signaling growing delays" | ❌ Unsupported — partial quarter, 28 deals; contradicted by the same tool in chat |
| 2 | "85 companies… 3,000 tickets" | ❌ Wrong — 3,000 tickets span 100 accounts; 204 sit outside the 85 |
| 3 | "nearly doubling" | ⚠️ Overstated — 1.58×, not 2× |
| 4 | Resolution times uniform | ✅ Correct interpretation, but omits critical (56.1 hrs) |
| — | All other figures (~30) | ✅ Exact, including 65.78% to two decimal places |

**Conclusion.** The generated summary is accurate at the level of individual numbers and unreliable at
the level of claims. Its errors are of the kind described in the Q Exploration Log: correct figures
assembled into a conclusion the data does not support, and two correct figures joined into an
incorrect sentence. It is useful as a drafting aid for someone who already knows the answers. It is
not safe to circulate unread.
